business_flow: User browses public site, registers/logs in, attempts access to /admin and /my-account with query parameter. Various static resource endpoints requested.
thought_process: I inspected each of the 22 HTTP entries. For each entry I applied the five checks: IDOR (BLA9), State Manipulation (BLA3), Sequence Bypass (BLA6), Shadow Endpoints (BLA10), Internal Disclosure (BLA8).

Only requests that include parameters or access to potentially sensitive endpoints can realistically show business logic vulnerabilities in this captured traffic. Many entries are static resource fetches with no parameters and provide no evidence of BLV in the traffic (status 0 or standard resources).
I must not invent vulnerabilities. I will only report endpoints where the captured request/response pair provides evidence or strong indication of a business-logic weakness per the framework.
I produce one finding per vulnerable endpoint observed in the traffic with a reproduction_guide containing payload_mutation and a curl_command using the required placeholders.

potential_vulnerabilities.description: Access to an undocumented or protected admin endpoint (/admin) returned 401 when accessed. The presence of a reachable /admin path indicates a shadow or sensitive function endpoint that may be abused if authentication is bypassed. The traffic shows a GET to /admin (Entry #3) producing 401 which suggests the endpoint exists and can be probed. This is evidence of a shadow/administrative endpoint being present and reachable to unauthenticated users, enabling discovery and further automated probing (BLA10).

reproduction_guide.payload_mutation: Send GET requests to /admin to enumerate behavior and try alternative methods (POST/OPTIONS) or parameter variations to discover functionality. Example: change no payload but alter method to POST or add common admin query parameters.

potential_vulnerabilities.description: Potential Insecure Direct Object Reference: /my-account endpoint accepts an 'id' query parameter (Entry #10: /my-account?id=attacker) and returned 200. This indicates the application uses a client-supplied identifier to render account pages. If ownership checks are missing server-side, an attacker could supply other users' identifiers to access their accounts (IDOR). The traffic shows a GET with id=attacker returning 200, demonstrating the parameter is honored.

reproduction_guide.payload_mutation: Change 'id' parameter from 'attacker' to another user's identifier, e.g., 'victim' or numeric user id.

potential_vulnerabilities.description: Shadow Function / Temporary-registration token endpoint: /register?temp-registration-token=... (Entry #14) shows the application accepts a 'temp-registration-token' GET parameter and returned 200. This parameterized registration URL suggests an undocumented or semi-private flow (temporary token acceptance) that could be manipulated to register or activate accounts without proper validation. Presence of long token in URL indicates a shadow function for temporary registration token handling.

reproduction_guide.payload_mutation: Change 'temp-registration-token' value to other token candidates or guessed values to enumerate valid tokens (e.g., replace token with another token or a short predictable string).

potential_vulnerabilities.description: Potential IDOR on product lookup: /product?productId=20 (Entry #11) uses a direct productId parameter to fetch product details. If product resources have sensitive attributes (pricing, inventory) that should be restricted, using a client-supplied productId without proper access controls could allow unauthorized access to restricted products. The captured traffic shows productId=20 returned 200, demonstrating the parameter is accepted.

reproduction_guide.payload_mutation: Change 'productId' from 20 to another product identifier (e.g., 21, 1, or a high-value/skewed id) to fetch other product details.
